In deciding as to the merits of the administration, does the hon. gentleman confine his opinion solely to legislation, or does he take into view the matter of administration generally?

Oh, well, I am not going to enter into a long discussion in regard to that; but when hon. members to my right consider the policy they have advocated and the principles we stand for, I do not see how in the world they can expect to get very much support from members in this part of the House. I am quite willing to turn to the other side and say they have been very slow in bringing forward some of those principles but we are going to support the Speech from the Throne. Hon. members to my right-I think the right hon. leader of the opposition said that he was quite prepared to support that speech.
Not at all.

The right hon. gentleman
says "not at all."
Will the hon. member be good enough to quote any such statement of mine? It has become the habit of some hon. members to be very loose in their statements.

We are getting used to the
right hon. leader of the opposition getting up and asking people to quote what he said. There is a general impression-
Take it back.
It is needless for me to take up time discussing that.

I ask the hon. member
to be good enough to withdraw the assertion that I said1 I would support the Speech from the Throne.

Mr. Speaker, I want some
more information before I withdraw that statement.
I rise to a point of order.
Order.

I have some authority in respect to the statements I have made. I have denied making this statement and I challenge the hon. gentleman to produce any quotation to support what he says. He has declined to do so, and I now ask and insist that he withdraw his statement.
Order.
Withdraw.
I would remind hon. members to my right that noise is not argument.
Withdraw.
I have nothing to withdraw. I intend to stay with the statement I have made.

Mr. Speaker, I ask for
your ruling. I propose that my rights shall not be abbreviated by the noise made by any hon. members in this House.

The statement made by
the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is that the right hon. leader of the opposition said that he was ready to support the measures mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. The right hon. leader of the opposition has taken exception to that statement. He states that there is not a tittle of evidence on which to base such a statement. I refer hon. members to paragraph 249 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, under rule 19, where I find the following:
It has been formally ruled by Speakers in the Canadian Commons that a statement by an honourable member respecting himself and peculiarly within his own knowledge must be accepted, but it is not unparliamentary to temperately criticize statements made by a member as being contrary to the facts; but no imputation of intentional falsehood is permissible.
In the present instance I consider the point raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition well taken. He denies in toto the assertion made by the hon. member for Brandon, and of course it is understood that when an hon. member denies having made a statement his word must be accepted by the House.

Adjournment oj the House

I am quite willing, after
your decision, Mr. Speaker, to withdraw what I have stated, but there is one point made absolutely clear, namely that the right hon. leader of the opposition does not accept the measures that are proposed in the Speech from the Throne. I can assure the House that some hon. members have been greatly misled in reference to what the right hon. leader of the opposition said when he was speaking in the debate on the Address.
I repeat again that in agreeing to this adjournment I feel it is a great disadvantage to all hon. members but I believe it will be in the best interests of the country and the best interests of the government that that adjournment should take place, and as a last word, I do hope that the press which is educating the people of this country will stop making statements and emphasizing them about the corruption and degradation that is taking place in this parliament.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members to my right
may laugh but to me it is no laughing matter. It is a serious matter that such things should occur. I know nothing about it. Do hon. members to my right know all about it? These newspapers are educating the people in this Dominion. The people have no other source of information and more harm is being done to the dignity of parliament through some of the editorials that are appearing in our papers at the present time than from anything which has taken place in this House during the time parliament has been sitting.

Mr. Speaker, in reference to the speech of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), I would observe that he "doth protest too much." He has given the figures of the electoral vote in the recent election. Now of this no one can have doubt, that as between the members on your right, Sir, and the party on your left, there was a Conservative majority. But we had a third party, supported not so largely as in 1921, but still having a very considerable following in this country, and if the hon. member for Brandon desires to associate his party with the Liberals well and good'. But let him be fair as between the two historical parties and let him attribute to his own party what he may fairly and triumphantly do, the control of this government.
I am opposed' to the motion for a long adjournment for this reason-and I endeavour to voice so far as I can the feeling of the man on the street, the outside public-that parliament was called for the despatch of
business, not for an adjournment of six weeks.
I venture to say that no more shocking spectacle has ever been presented in connection with parliamentary government than that which we have witnessed recently in this very country. It recalls to my mind a gibe of Disraeli under somewhat similar circumstances, when he pictured the government of that day in this way. He said that from a certain point along the shores of South America you can see a range of extinct volcanoes, from which not one flame flickers from a single pallid crest. So the government sits to-day. And why this motion for adjournment? The hon. Minister of Justice said he had no opportunity of addressing the House upon the motion. What difference would it make if he had had the opportunity? Is there anyone in the House who does not know the purpose of the adjournment? It is to endeavour to reanimate a moribund government and for no other purpose and if that be so-and this is a point I would stress-why is it that this so-called government has met parliament? It is a government it is true; it is in office; decimated though it be, it is yet a government. If it is a fact that it is unable to function, why did it assemble parliament for the despatch of business? I believe rightly or wrongly that the nerves of the people of Canada are in a state of tension. I believe that the business of this country is being halted for lack of confidence in the stability of government, and the longer we delay getting on with business and determining who are to form the government and manage the affairs of Canada for some years to come, the longer will business be in a state of uncertainty, and the longer will capital hesitate to invest. For these reasons I propose to vote against the adjournment.

Mr. Speaker, coming from the Toronto district I wish to lay before the House the necessity of ending the deadlock which exists in this country to-dhy.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to vote against the motion for the adjournment of the House until March 15. I see no necessity for such an adjournment, with the economic problems that are to-day confronting the country. We have a government without a head. We have the very negative of a government. No province in the Do-

Adjournment of the House
minion is suffering more acutely from economic ills at the present time than Ontario. To-day we find that province is without a single cabinet minister in this honourable House the first time since confederation. During the past three or four years deputations have been coming to Ottawa from British Columbia, from the prairie provinces and from the Maritime provinces with their declarations of rights, and I think it is pretty nearly time the old province of Ontario had a ginger group in this House. Then the other sections of the country would soon realize that they are very well off compared with the province from which I come. As one of the representatives from the great industrial district of Toronto, I protest against this House adjourning without having made any attempt to solve the economic problems that beset Canada and Ontario to-day.
What this country needs, Mr. Speaker, is a revival-an economic revival headed by a revivalist. They have had such a revival in Great Britain; the political party of Mr. Bonar Law and Mr. Stanley Baldwin, which had not been in power its full term, gave up office with four or five years yet to run. Why? Because they thought it was time to consult the people, and that a time and tide had come in the affairs of the country to settle the great economic problems which were confronting the motherland. We in Canada need a revival headed by a revivalist which will solve the practical problems which this country has to solve to-day. I believe the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is the revivalist needed to head this revival as he is the head of the main group in this House and would to-day have been asked to form a cabinet if we had representation by population in Canada, but we have not. The large cities and towns which pay the bulk of the taxes of the country were kept from the exercise of their franchise by the great gerrymander of the 1924 redistribution bill.
I believe my right hon. leader is the proper person to lead such a revival as we need to-day in Canada. I come from an industrial part of Canada; the Toronto district is the home of industries of all kinds, as well as mixed farming and market gardening. Today Ontario is suffering as no other province of the Dominion is suffering from the lack of adequate protection from unemployment; from stagnation and from the evils which exist in Canada to-day through the failure of the government to bring the National Policy up to date and to bring forward a

proper safeguarding of industries act for the people of Canada.
Protection is not a dead thing; it is a living reality; it is the only question before the people in this country to-day. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) was speaking the other day of the immigration problem and the railway problem. Those are not the problems the people want settled. The right solution of the tariff problem and a proper safeguarding of industries will automatically solve all the problems referred to by my hon. friend. No city in the country pays more taxes than does the city of Toronto. If we had representation by .population we would have fifteen members from that city in this House. Toronto was built up by protection, as the whole province of Ontario has been built up by protection. The revenue derived by this government from the city of Toronto is nearly 8100,000,000; $60,000,000 comes from customs receipts; nearly $6,000,000 from postal receipts, and over $10,000,000 from income taxes. Central Canada is paying SI per cent of all the taxes of Canada to-day, and these two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec are demanding some additional protection for their industries. Protection is not a dead thing; it should be brought up to date in every province to meet the changed conditions and local exigencies brought about by the disturbance of industrial equilibrium. I support protection not for the manufacturers only, not for the bankers only, not for the farmers only, but for everyone, for national reasons and on the ground of patriotism. The principles of protection alone can establish economic unity among the provinces of Canada. The government of the day may be compared to a baseball team; it had a very -bad road trip which wound up on October 29 last. The government then met the House on January 7th without a programme to present.
Even speaking from the partisan point of view, while I do not pretend to know very much about politics I think it is bad politics from the government's point of view for the Liberal party to propose an adjournment until March 15. The country will blame them for it; the unrest will go on, unemployment will continue, there will still be the lack of proper safeguarding of industries; and you will have stagnation in the land; you are just postponing the evil day. It seems to me that what the Liberal party needs very badly at the present time is a professional coach, as they are called. We have a government without a head and without a policy, and I say it is a

Adjournment oj the House
merely negative government. I have been here for four or five sessions, and I may say to my Liberal friends of the left that I do not know what they are doing in that corner of the House. There is no use in their staying there any longer and playing any further puss-in-the-corner. Their proper place is away over in the other corner of the House beside the so-called Independent member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I have the utmost respect for the Progressives personally but none at all for their platform. If we ever had a sample of what the actors call "cheap political vaudeville" in this House we have it in the person of the genial hon. member for Labelle calling himself an Independent when he is a Liberal first, last, and all the time.
The Globe to-day has over its report a big headline saying that in the division last night the "Liberal party had a majority of ten and that all Progressives joined in voting against the Meighen amendment." Of course they did, and why not? Did anybody expect them to vote any other way? I have never known during my four or five years in this House of any display of independence on the part of the Progressive party. The only time such a spirit was shown was the other night when four or five Progressives voted with the opposition, reducing the majority of the government to three. But those Progressives soon lost that independence, and the whole Progressive party went over holus-bolus to the government last night-they should stay there. The Progressives are about as independent as the hon. member for Labelle; like him they have never been anything else but Liberal, and I predict they never will change. The government will never want for eight or ten votes so long as there are any Progressives in the House to support them. The same may be said of the two gentlemen who call themselves labour representatives. I respect them personally, but who authorized those two gentlemen to call themselves the Labour party, and to say that they represent the working classes? The fact that they call themselves the Labour party doesn't make them a Labour party. They do not represent the working classes of the city of Winnipeg, I may tell them, let alone the working classes from coast to coast in this country.
The duty of this House is to restore responsible government and the two-party system; to abolish referendums and useless commissions. The group system of government, both in the federal house and in provincial legislatures, has been nothing but a complete failure. The group system of government as
represented by the so-called Drury Farmer-Labour government of Ontario gave this province the worst form of government any province ever saw in the history of the British Empire. There was corruption of all kinds, and everything of that nature. The so-called Drury government was driven from office by the vote of the people without their having carried out a single plank of their platform. Neither have the Progressives carried out a single plank of the platform they were elected on or of the National Council of Agriculture. Their platform was merely one to get in on, not to stand on.
When the Progressives were in power in Ontario our debt increased by leaps and bounds as well as maintenance charges, and they all but destroyed the investment of 200 millions of the municipalities in cheap hydro light and power. The sooner Progressive members of this House wake up to the fact that they can no longer put anything over on the voters in the polling booths and constituencies the better for the Progressives and the better for the country as a whole. The people of this country are going to follow those of England in voting for principles. So long as a party stands by its principles it will continue in strength, But when they desert their principles, as the Liberal and the Progressive parties have done, there always comes a time when the people will assert themselves. I have this to say of the party and group systems. The critics of party no doubt have much to allege against the party system, and some of it not without justice. Party leads to unreasonable and unpatriotic extremes of thought and action in the excitement of our political struggles. It leads sometimes to forgetfulness of the objects for which parties exist and which alone justify their existence-the greatness of the country and the welfare of its people. It leads often and most frequently to an exaggeration of our differences and to the minimizing of the great mass of agreement that in the past has been common to all parties. But I will say this to critics of party: do not judge parties only by defects; judge them also by merits. The alternative to party is groups, sections, interests and classes. I do not say none of these affects the course of action of party, but I do say that the broad allegiance to the party of your choice keeps those smaller, narrower, and baser motives in check, and that it was a bad day for this country when it abandons the party system which our free parliamentary institutions had developed, and slipping into that system of little groups and sections which gives the

Adjournment oj the House
largest play to petty interests and takes the least notice of the great issues of the day.
That has been found to be true. In Great Britain the group system proved a failure. It led the country into all kinds of economic ills, and almost destroyed the British Empire. England during that time lost a large number of orders to the Hamburg shipping yards; it was rapidly losing its supremacy in shipbuilding, as well as its national stability and its industries were being ruined.
What this country wants is that parliament should continue in session and grapple with the problems that are facing us. If the government is not able to grapple with these problems, let them dissolve parliament and go to the country. If we cannot win I would far rather see a Liberal government returned to power than have such a makeshift government of groups and classes as we have at the present time. The party system is the only system for any country. The war taught Canada one lesson, and that was the value of team work, and if we carried into peace the lessons we learned in the war, all would be well. In the war, merchants, prince, and pauper worked together side by side, and if we carry on in that spirit we shall be able to solve the economic problems that are facing us. I contend that if a national policy is a necessity, not a luxury, in time of war, it is a necessity in time of peace as well, and the basis of that policy is protection-protection diversified and suited to the economic needs of every province and adjusted to the local circumstances; in other words, a national policy brought up to date. Canada has grown up under the National Policy. We want a policy of protection that lives and moves and has its being for the upbuilding of a united Canada, and the principle of protection alone can make for a united Canada for Canadians. Such a policy will stop the exodus from this country and bring our boys back from the United States; it will promote migration within the empire; it will eliminate the deficits on our railways, solve unemployment, take care of our raw material and preserve to us for all time to come the magnificent heritage that we have in the products of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mines. It will make for a united, prosperous and contented people and make Canada a country for Canadians. No apology is necessary for protection or for what it would do for Canada. Ontario and Quebec are paying eighty per cent of the taxes of the Dominion, and Quebec, just like Ontario, is a protectionist province. It has been built up. like Ontario, on the National Policy. In days gone by

Upper and Lower Canada always got on well together. Baldwin and Lafontaine united the people and when a candidate was defeated in Quebec he could always find a seat in York and vice versa. Quebec has some good protectionist papers on both sides of politics. I would like to quote from a leading French-Canadian paper, Le Soleil, in an issue of last year:
To be worthy of the name, protection as a policy ought to be applied to the interests and well-being of society as a whole and not to the interests of the .few. It ought to embrace all the professions, and all who fail within the categories of commerce, wholesale and retail; of all workers, whether they are engaged in stores or offices; of all women and children from whom the necessities of life are procured-provisions and clothing. In a word, protection ought to be for all classes of society. This provides a problem which cannot be solved in modifications of the tariffs of one kind and another, however important they may be.
Wise words-protection for all classes and provinces. That is a good protectionist doctrine. It advocates bringing the National Policy up to date and applying it to the whole country starting with the provinces down by the sea and on right through to the coast. With all the problems that are facing us, and in view of the great sacrifice of time on the part of men who have come here from the extremes of Canada, I think it would be bad policy, even from a Liberal standpoint, to adjourn this parliament for six weeks, thus making our coming here all to no purpose, and making a football of any effort to solve our problems.
We should have a maximum tariff, not a minimum one, so that we can prevent this country from being the happy hunting ground for American millionaires who come here and grab our raw materials, our timber, our mineral wealth and our water powers. What we need is a policy that will1 prevent the foolish export of our valuable raw materials, and allow them to be manufactured here at home, thus creating employment for our own people. I am further of the opinion that it is just as fair and honourable and just to use the weapon of the tariff to protect our industries from the dumping of foreign countries, as it is to call out the militia to defend our land against the invasion of armed forces. If the Liberal party in this House will look across to England they will see what has become of the Liberal party in the Old Country. It is practically wiped out. The Liberal party in this country has not had a settled policy on the tariff since 1896. "The principles of Liberalism" were often on the lips of Mr. Mackenzie King in North YorK. On tariff matters he has been everything by

Adjournment oj the House
fits and starts, and nothing long. Particularly, I say, is that true of his attitude with regard to the tariff, which he has continually nibbled at, taking off a little bit here and a little bit there, thereby creating unrest, unemployment and instability.

I would ask the hon.
gentleman to keep a little closer to the subject matter. His remarks may have some relation to the motion before the House, but I cannot see it.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I understood that considerable latitude was being allowed in this debate, and I contend the tariff is the main problem to settle.
It as not in the interest of the people of Canada that this parliament should adjourn until the 15th of March, in view of the national economic problems that are pressing for solution. We have an unemployment problem, for instance, in this country, which to-day is very acute. The unemployment situation lias grown out of our failure to have a proper protective tariff and a safeguarding of industries act. Unemployment is also due to the shipping of our raw materials across :o the United States, where they are manufactured instead of being manufactured here at home, giving work to our own peopie. Canada is being made a dumping ground for the cheap, shoddy goods of the United States and continental Europe. Departmental stores in my own city are full of cheap German and American goods, with the result that we have unemployment in that city. That is one of the problems we should take up immediately and solve before allowing any adjournment. What is the policy of the government on unemployment? We had a Minister of Labour last session, and he said that the government of Canada, under the British North America Act, had nothing to do with unemployment ; that it was a matter for the provinces and municipalities. The federal government has jurisdiction in matters of trade and commerce, immigration, banking and finance, and transportation, and it is their function to relieve unemployment, or make some effort to do so.
Now, why should we adjourn, in view of the condition of affairs which exists in the country to-day? We 'have two representatives of the Labour party in this House, and what have they to say about unemployment? They are supporting the government and also the Progressives-and the latter are practically free traders. The hon. member for Rose-town (Mr. Evans) admitted it the other night.

He is one of the most courageous men on the Progressive benches, and he got up and said point-blank that he was in favour of free trade. I ask both the Labour members here how they expect to solve the unemployment problem in this country by supporting the policy of free trade as against protection? How are old age pensions to be paid if free trade comes into force? How do my hon. friends expect to solve any of the problems that affect the working class under such a policy? And yet it is proposed to adjourn the House and make a political football of all these questions-and the Labour members consent to that course being taken.
Let me remind these gentlemen that the late Mr. Gompers was one of the most astute labour leaders this continent ever knew. He did not believe in a Labour party; he believed in working .within the two great political parties in the United States, the Republican and the Democratic parties, with the result that he secured the adoption of practical measures that were in the interests of the working classes in the land of his adaption. I do not know of any country where higher wages are paid to-day than in the United States. The former Minister of Labour, Mr. Murdock, said last session that twenty millions of men were out of work in the country to the south. I took the trouble to write to Mr. Davis, Secretary of Labour, and in reply he informed me that there were only a million men out of work there out of a population of 110,000,000. I tell my hon. friends of the Labour party that they do not represent the cause of labour when they support the policies to which they are now giving adherence. They cannot truly represent labour when they are supporting free trade principles. Protection is the greatest friend labour has in this country. Look at what has been accomplished for labour in the way of legislation in Ontario. When the country gets into any kind of economic trouble it always sends for the Conservative party to get it out of the difficulty. Clan my hon. friends point to a single labour organization in the United States that opposes protection and favours free trade? No, Mr. Speaker, every labour organization in that country has consistently supported the principle of protection, with the result that labour is in a strong position in the United States to-day.
Our Progressive friends are fond of referring to the Old Country. You will not find Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin proposing to adjourn the Imperial parliament when there are great public questions to be settled. No, he is now engaged in the solution of economic problems
Adjournment oj the House

over there and is getting capital and labour together. May I be permitted to say that Great Britain is coming to adopt the protective policy also? Under free trade as they have it over there the unemployment question is a most serious one. Over a million of men are out of work in Great Britain, many of them returned men. Has free trade solved the unemplojunent question over there? Has it solved the dole problem? Has it solved the question of hours of labour? Has England under free trade been able to abolish the Poor law? To all these questions the answer must be no.
Why should this parliament adjourn? Who is asking for it? Has the government to-day any mandate from the people asking it to postpone to March 15 further consideration of the many economic problems before us- so little done, so much^ to do-problems of settling deficits and reducing the taxes? When I look into classical history I say to the government, "Beware the ides of March." As a result of the policy which the government has decided to pursue, there will be more unemployment, unrest and stagnation in Canada and we shall get nowhere with the problems that await solution. The unemployed have asked for bread and you are going to give them a stone, to wit, a postponement for six weeks of consideration of any action on their behalf.
I wish to say in conclusion that what this country wants at the present time is a revival, and I believe we have a revivalist, who will conduct an economic revival, in the person of my right hon. leader. For that reason, coming from an industrial district where unemployment is rife and where the industrial equilibrium has been unbalanced for a considerable time, I oppose the motion for an adjournment. At a time when the present government is so apathetic I commend to its notice the vigorous action which Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin and his government are adopting in Great Britain. Mr. Baldwin is endeavouring to bring capital and labour together. He is going up and down the country, meeting all classes of the people, in an endeavour to solve the economic problems of the old land. We in this country are not a practical people. We take a long time to settle our problems; we think too much of party and too little of the welfare of Canada. For that reason the problems which confront us here remain unsolved and will continue to remain in that state as long as we have the present government.

Canada is essentially Liberal-minded and Mackenzie King was given a mandate on October 29. It may have been a feeble one, due to certain psychological factors, but still it was a mandate. It called for action. It called for more than the glueing of political ears to the political ground for an indefinite period.
Mackenzie King should have found a seat for himself long ago and got down to business.
What Canada wants down in Ottawa is a leader, not a weather vane.
Those remarks from an enthusiastic Liberal newspaper two months ago apply more fittingly to-day than they ever did before. The purpose of this adjournment is to enable the weather vane to figure out the way the wind is blowing in the prairie provinces. He is down there now with his ears glued to the ground endeavouring to establish a seat, while the business of this country is drifting along. If you talk with men of responsibility, you find that capital is hesitant in its investments; that there is business inactivity, political demoralization, confusion and a general mess in the country. Yet the government proposes to add to this by an extension of six weeks by way of an adjournment without any attempt being made to handle the public business.
I shall be interested in hearing what explanation the government has to make. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) made some explanation. " Why," he said, " if w'e were sitting here during the next six weeks when the by-elections were on, they would be making political speeches and we would not be able to do any business." There are 245 hon. members, here from all parts of Canada, and we are face to face with problems of the most serious nature, some of which should be discussed by members for the elucidation of their fellow members and worked at by committees that could be carried on to the great advantage of parliament in the solution of such problems. To say that we cannot do business in the face of this situation is nonsense, and as a member from British Columbia I am here to make the most vigorous protest against any adjournment. When I go back to my constituents in the city of Vancouver and visit people in other parts of Canada, I propose to bring to their attention the course which the government is now carrying on, the sham and farce of the whole thing, and the manner in which the business of the country has been delayed and held up for no other purpose than the hope in my hon, friends' hearts of bettering the political situation.
I wonder why the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has not given us some reasons in support of his motion. I have been only four years in this House, but my short ex-

perience and my modicum of reason would lead me to believe that on such an important motion as this, the first thing the leader of the House would do would be to establish the grounds upon which he was asking 245 hon. members to disperse to their homes and wait for six w-eeks. Is it the intention of the Minister of Justice or of any other mem-9 p.m. ber of the government to give us that information before the vote is taken, or, are they to sit there silent, knowing that they have a binding agreement, an unalterable arrangement, with our Progressive friends which will cause them to support the government in the vote without any explanations at all? Not only parliament, but the people of Canada are entitled to an explanation, and it is to be hoped that the government will furnish some reasons for a course of action which seems to me to be unprecedented.
I desire also to refer to another portion of the report of the Prime Minister's speech at Prince Albert. I do so because, as a member of this House, I regret that the Prime Minister of this country should take a course of action and a line of campaign which one might expect from a demagogue rather than from a leader of a government. This report may be wrong, but I quote these words as given in the Ottawa Citizen this morning. This is what the Prime Minister said:
What we were fighting was, not the policy of the Conservative party-
Nobody knows better than he that such a statement is simply rubbish.
-we were fighting money, millions of dollars put in by financial interests to get control .in this country. I say that so long as we have men who are selfishly seeking their own interests, who are prepared to spend money in that way, so long the interests of the people will never be safe.
Hear, hear.

Some hon. members and,
in particular the Solicitor General, say "hear, hear." Does he really and honestly believe there is any truth in that statement?
Absolutely.
I know as regards Vancouver the Liberal party were fighting ourselves and our policies, and not any millions, by any means.
You are an island.

You are so near the deep blue seas, politically speaking, that you may want to be an island yourself before the vote is over. I refer to this because, having considerable respect personally for Mr. Mackenzie

Adjournment of the House
King, I think it is regrettable that the leader of any party, especially the Prime Minister of this country, should stand before our nine million people and seek to arouse their antagonisms, prejudices and dislikes in this fashion. This savours of methods which were used in the reports and posters cited in the speech of the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Doucet). There are present the same psychologies, the same ideas. The Prime Minister goes to the western plains, meets the hard working farmers there, many of whom are no doubt struggling to eke out an existence, and, standing in the dignity of his position as head of the government, he virtually tells those people:	"You are poor people;
I am your saviour. We shall have to fight these great robber barons holding these millions in Montreal."
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends say,
"hear, hear." I think that is cheap politics. That is the politics of the demagogue, and the sooner a protest is made against it the better in the interest of public life and of the party system in this country. It is a bad thing.
I conclude by repeating that, as a member from British Columbia, I have come to Ottawa three thousand miles to assist in transacting the business of this country. We are here ready and willing to do it. We are here ready to participate to the best of our ability in the solution of problems and we consider it is the duty of the government-having had three months to prepare their programme, having placed that programme specifically before the people in the Speech from the Throne with problems that must go before committees, and knowing full well that they are not going to prepare any business programme during the next four or five weeks, when they will be engaged on the hustings endeavouring to elect their ministers in the by-elections- it is the duty of the government not to adjourn but to go ahead with the business of the country. The whole procedure is, in fact, a pretence, a sham and a farce. The course of the government is to endeavour to disentangle itself from a political mess which it should not be in because it should have resigned after the last election. It is one of a series of steps which will end in the government being obliged to resign because the popular will is against it.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure those members who have a sense of humour must have
been amused by two incidents this afternoon- one supplied by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the other by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I was greatly amused when the Minister of Justice complained that the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) had taken his place in the debate. I have sat in the House for I think nine sessions with the hon. gentleman, and I have never known him to be of such a retiring nature. I never discovered him giving place to any other member in those nine sessions. While in opposition he was perhaps the most aggressive member in the whole house. I recollect on one occasion when his friends boasted in the corridors that he was going to get the scalp of my right, hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who was then leader of the government, but the latter-turned the tables on him and had his scalp dangling at his belt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never entertained such an idea.
I mention that to show the aggressive character of my hon. friend.
Both of them are bald.

To-day he complained in a childlike manner that someone else had taken his place in the debate. I think that is the most amusing incident that has happened so far this session. I was equally amused by my hon. friend from Labelle, whose paternal admonitions to his Liberal friends were followed by a statement that he was going to wait and see what their policy was and the reasons for the adjournment prior to making up his mind, but before he sat down he had pledged his vote as fully as it was possible for any member to do. I am afraid my hon. friend from Labelle talks a good deal at random, Sir, and on that account I feel that he must be excused for his lapse this afternoon.
I was sorry to hear my hon. friend the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) refer to the insinuations and suspicions that have been made and aroused as a result of the vote on the first amendment of this session. If people outside the House are talking about corruption, I do not think it is going to add to the dignity of parliament for such ill-grounded suspicions, I trust, to be discussed here. We should be above that sort of thing, and I think if my hon. friend had had more experience in public life he would not have expressed himself as he did to-day, because it certainly detracts from the
Adjournment oj the House

dignity of parliament and the respect with which it should be regarded.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I oppose this adjournment.
Why?

Well, this is one reason, of many. What the country is suffering from to-day is a lack of confidence in the government. That was manifested in the vote on October 29. If the government has any policies that its members think will restore confidence in them, it is their duty to bring those policies forward and have them discussed, so that confidence may be inspired in the commercial circles of Canada. There can be no greater injury to a country than a loss of confidence on the part of those men who have it in their power to begin a revival of trade, and any party or any group of men that may be guilty of measures which stand in the way of a return of that confidence are doing a very grave injury to their country. We were told that parliament was going to be convened at the earliest possible moment. But, Sir, we find that the real work of parliament is to begin over two months after the date set for the opening of the session; the proposal now to adjourn for six weeks throws back the opening of parliament for real business to March 15 instead of January 7. The commercial interests of the Dominion-and I submit that they are of some importance and are to be considered

looked forward to the opening of parliament as a time when something would be done to give them an indication whether there was any reason on their part for a revival of confidence in the government, or in the party that ought to be in office, but instead of that all parliamentary business has been put aside.
To my mind there has never been such a confession of incompetence on the part of any government that this country has ever had equal to that which is displayed in this motion. The Liberal party came to this House declaring that although they were a minority group, they still had the right and the power to carry on. To-day they confess that they are without the power to carry on, and they ask this House to adjourn for six weeks. It causes me, Mr. Speaker, to go back in my memory to the founders of the Liberal party and1 to wonder what they would have done under similar circumstances. Can anyone imagine Brown, or Blake, or Mackenzie, or Laurier acting as this government has acted? Beaten at the polls, with a large and decisive popular majority against them, they still cling to office, making a bargain by which
fMr. Hocken.}
they surrender all their political principles. This they do to retain power. Can anyone imagine Laurier doing that? The men who founded the Liberal party were men of strong convictions, they were men who went down fighting for those convictions rather than cling to office by surrendering them. I knew something of those men. I was very young, of course, but I recall the type of man that Alexander Mackenzie was.
Some hon. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

Some of my hon. friends opposite laugh. Well, he has left it on record that he was a little too honest for the rank and file of his own party. He stands out today as a man incorruptible, ready to suffer for his convictions. Those who surrounded him at that time were men of the same type. The Hon. George Brown was a doughty fighter, a man who fought more vigorously, for his principles than perhaps any of his contemporaries; but he would1 not cling to the emoluments and honours of office when the popular majority was against him. To him, such action was impossible. And no man of spirit would do it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was such a man. He had a pride in his own reputation, and he had some regard for reputation of his party. And I want to tell my hon. friends opposite that what they are doing to-day will react upon their party in the future to a degree that they do not now apprehend. I will give them a percedent for it. No group of men can exhibit themselves to the country as insincere, as office grabbers, as dingers to the emoluments and honours of office in spite of the popular vote, without suffering disaster from their own party. I had an experience, Mr. Speaker, in my own election.
Did you do that?

No. I may not be any good, but I have some convictions and whether they are good or not I stick to them, like my right hon. leader and the Conservative party. I recall to my hon. friends the course of the government of the province of Ontario about the year 1900. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that when Sir Wilfrid Laurier organized his government in 1896 he brought Sir Oliver Mowat to Ottawa as his Minister of Justice. The government of Ontario then fell into the hands of Mr. Hardy, a fine, honourable, splendid type of Liberal. Mr. Hardy unfortunately died, and was succeeded by Mr. Ross. Those who know the Scottish character tell me that Mr. Ross, being a Highlander, was unable to fight his friends,

Adjournment of the House
so there gathered around him a machine which won one election after another by the most disgraceful and discreditable methods ever practised in this country. The result was, Mr. Speaker, that in succeeding elections ms government got down to a majority of one but still' hung on. The result of all this clinging to office, which was accomplished partly by bargaining with members who had been elected for other parties and partly by electoral crookedness, was that his party was swept from office, and from that day to this the Liberal party has been nothing but-an insignificant group in the legislature of the province of Ontario. What is the deduction, Sir? Is it not that the decent Liberals, the decent people whether Liberals or Conservatives or Progressives, will not stand for that sort of thing? They will not stand for selfishness and insincerity on the part of their representatives, and this government to-day is laying the foundation for the ruin of the great Liberal party. I venture the prediction that this is the most unfortunate thing ever done for Liberalism. I am not concerned with its preservation. If I were speaking for this group I would say that we should rejoice over what this government is doing and is trying to do, because we know it is just the prelude to absolute disaster for that party. Another election must come; it ought to come now, and this government should resign. It has not a mandate from the people, but on the contrary has received the utmost condemnation. This government should relinquish the reins of office to another party, regardless of whether or not that other party can Carry on, and that party should decide whether or not there should be an election and when the election should be held. There must be an election. The Globe, the chief Liberal organ in the Dominion of Canada, calls for a new election. It is speaking not for this party but for my hon. friends opposite. The paper founded by George Brown, which has been the Liberal organ for eighty odd years, appreciates the situation; it has regard for the future of its party, and it calls upon that party to resign and have another election to clear the air. Let some party receive a mandate and carry on the government of this country.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that the actions of the government have worked great injury. If the House adjourns for six weeks and leaves the business of the country in a state of confusion, the insincerity of the government will react against themselves. I sympathize with my hon. friendis who have to travel to Vancouver, and I do not believe
my hon. friends the Progressives want an adjournment. How they came to be persuaded into making that bargain I do not know; perhaps it was as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said, that they persuaded the so-called government of the day to formulate their policy. In other words, they said, "You take our policy and we will take your adjournment." All these hon. gentlemen must go back to their farms, and they cannot do very much there during the next six weeks except to feed the pigs and milk the cows. I have on the order paper a resolution, one paragraph of which I will read to the House in order to impress upon hon. members the importance of this question. It reads:
That a committee composed of members of this House be appointed to investigate our present sources of supply of anthracite and bituminous coal. The dependability of such sources, and whether the prices paid by the Canadian consumer is fair and reasonable, and to also enquire as to the methods of mining and delivering Canadian coal in the best and cheapest way to all parts of the Dominion, for the purpose of giving employment to our workmen, freight to our transportation companies, and thus effecting a saving of money now spent for tfiis commodity in other countries.
That is an important resolution and one that should be dealt with at the earliest possible moment. I have no doubt that if the government adjourn for six weeks it will be practically impossibe for a committee of this House to deal with this question in any definite manner during the present session of parliament. It is not a question that can be dealt with by any individual or municipality or local government; it is a question for this parliament and the members of this parliament to decide definitely at this very session, in order that the people of central Canada may have delivered to them at the lowest possible cost, the fuel that is so badly needed in that part of the country. But the gang, presumably-I use the word presumably, although I am quite certain in my own mind about it, and I think proof can be brought t o support it-presumably the gang under the control of Bisaillon beat him to it by twenty-four hours and stole the trunks that were in the custody of the chief constable.
But that is not the whole story. One Bud Harris, a coloured man, who was one of the gang implicated in all this rascality and criminality, had $3,000 coming to him, and they would not pay him. He then intimated that he was going to disclose the rascality of the smuggling gang, and what happened to him? If you will turn back the files of the Montreal papers you will find where the body of a coloured man was found wired up with wire and weighted with weights in the Back river. I think from the description I give of this case hon. members will recall it. That was the body of Bud Harris, the coloured member of this gang. That was what he got for intimating he would squeal on the smug- * gling gang in Montreal. Mr. Speaker, do you wonder that I emphasize this: that with the knowledge of these things, with the knowledge of the character of this man Bisaillon, with the knowledge of these activities of Giroux and others, this government preserved them in their office since last February with positive knowledge before them, and with equal

knowledge of their rascality, put this man Bisaillon in the premier office of the customs service-the known king of smugglers in tire Dominion of Canada. And then this government comes to this House and asks for confidence! Yes, asks for an adjournment so that I can be prevented from investigating this matter before a parliamentary committee <5f this House.
What, are you talking about? Puie bunkum!
Mr. Speaker, I hope you are not missing the eloquent language of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) .
Order. I remember years ago a Speaker's ruling to the effect that the word "humbug" was not parliamentary. The word "bunk" I should say is certainly not in the King's English.
I said bunkum.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to give considerable latitude under the circumstances. Now I leave this gang of criminals, not only associates of, but let me emphasize it, all of them under the supreme control and leadership of Bisaillon.
Now I may be asked, what about this wholesale smuggling? Is there wholesale smuggling? I want to say here, on my responsibility as a member of this House, that there is the most flagrant, organized, persistent, wholesale smuggling in the border towns along the province of Quebec and the American boundary, and again I say, so that the members from Quebec will not think I am picking on their province, that the same thing, perhaps in a lesser degree, exists along the boundary of Maine and along the boundary in other places. But here, Sir, we have it erected into a legalized traffic, a regular occupation or vocation, and with the individuals practising it known to the government, with the individuals who are carrying it on from day to day walking the streets as respected1 citizens, and daily, monthly, and weekly, defrauding the exchequer of this country of hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of dollars I am well within the mark-millions of dollars. I could, Sir-any man could-within a week have these men arrested, seize some of their effects, and1 endeavour to secure a portion, some small portion, of the funds of which this country has been defrauded. It is not a difficult task. I have under my hands a list of their names, I have them here. All

To give an illustration, the other day one New York firm boasted of having received from a Canadian firm, the name of which I have under my hand, an order for S120,000 worth of cotton goods, and not an ounce of it paid customs duty. I say that no prosecutions of any account have been conducted and I charge the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General with the responsibility for carrying on prosecutions of this kind.

I was proceeding with
the Giroux case. This man is tide surveyor, one of the chief officers in the port of Mont-

real. In the Rex vs. Lortie-St. George case, he is one of the individuals whom the judge warned that he was committing perjury. The Dominion Bridge Company imported a cargo of coal which was cleared through Giroux and Sons, Giroux andl Sons being Giroux, the customs officer, tide surveyor of the port of Montreal, his firm, Giroux and Sons, being customs brokers in the same port. The Dominion Bridge Company cleared this cargo of coal, giving a cheque for $1,800 in payment of the duty on it. On checking up their coal invoices they found that they had overpaid their duty by $100 or $200-1 will not quibble over the amount-and they applied for a rebate to the collector of customs at Montreal, who is credited to be and is, I believe, an honest man although he has been shorn of all authority. The collector turned up the records of the department in the possession of this government, because all of these are government records, and he told the Dominion Bridge Company that this cargo was cleared free as anthracite and that nothing was paid into the exchequer. Do I have to repeat that to let it sink into the minds of hon. gentlemen? Mr. Wilson referred to a moment ago, knows all about this. He went to Montreal; he touched up the long distance telephone and things got busy. What happened? Giroux, the tide surveyor of Montreal, put up his own cheque or at least repaid the $1,800 that he had stolen from this government. That is one case in recent times. W'hat I am coming to is this, that this man Giroux and scores of others,, have been perpetrating these thefts and frauds for years.

If the hon. gentleman
knows as much as he says he does, why does he not put a formal demand upon any court of justice and prosecute the men he knows to be guilty?

Again I suggest to you,
Mr. Speaker, that a request, a suggestion of that kind is so absurd and ludicrous that it is unworthy of any further consideration or thought.
That is easy to say.

That is not easy to say.
Let me elaborate. Surely, this country has not come to the pass where a member of parliament must go down to a province or city and start prosecutions against those who are stealing from the government within the knowledge of that government. I am arraigning this government before the bar of public opinion and not going into police court prosecutions. No one is going to bluff me with any suggestions such as that.

If the hon. member has
any special charge to make' against any member of the government or any member of this parliament, let him put his seat at stake and we will take him up on it.

There seem to be many
hon. gentlemen who are desirous of getting this seat of mine. It might be opportune just to make an observation on this seat that I happen to possess, and which, by the way, I have represented in this House for some seventeen sessions. I made my return honestly the other day. My opponent who spent probably twice as much money as my committee made no return at all. That probably accounts for the anxiety to get control of my seat.
I turn now to another phase of this question. I have given some illustrations, and only a few, of the criminalities of officers of the government and I will repeat that abundant evidence of this has been filed and is within the general knowledge of the senior officers of the crown. What did the government do? About a year ago the Minister of Customs of that period started an investigation. The Minister of Justice asked from his place a moment ago: Does the hon. gentleman not know that we have conducted investigations? Yes, this is one. Whom did they send to investigate? Mr. Inspector R. P. Clerk. Who is he? In 1911 Chief Inspector Busby, than whom there is no better officer in the service-does anybody dispute that? Will the Minister of Customs now pay a little tribute to Chief Inspector Busby?

If my hon. friend wants
me to interrupt him, I certainly pay tribute to Chief Inspector Busby, who would be
inspecting the port of Montreal to-day if he was not sick and at home. His assistant is there doing the work in his place.

Mr. Busby has been
sedulously kept out of the port of Montreal for three years, and my hon. friend knows that.
By whom?
By the government through the late Minister of Customs, Mr. Bureau.
Oh, oh.

Some hon. members say: "Oh, oh." Let me repeat that Mr. Bureau retired from the government largely because of some of these things with which I am dealing. But let us go on with Mr. Clerk. Who is he? In 1911 Chief Inspector Busby investigated the port of Montreal, with the result that Mr. Clerk was reduced or demoted,
placed in a minor and junior position because of some irregularities or incapacity or faults :n his administration. When Mr. Bureau took charge-and I want to say this government is responsible for Mr. Bureau's actions; they will not deny that-I merely say Mr. Bureau, because if I say the government, the ministers one after the other will assert they knew nothing about it-when this government came into power they appointed Mr. Clerk inspector of the port and district of Montreal-Mr. Clerk who had been demoted by the previous government for irregularities in his administration. From that day forward Mr. Busby, the best customs inspector that Canada probably ever had, was excluded by this government from the port of Montreal. Clerk is totally unqualified for his job; he never wias fitted for it.
What was the result of his appointment? The present collector-a splendid gentleman, an honourable, an honest man-has simply been a figurehead drawing his salary, while Clerk, Bisaillon, Giroux, these other men, have administered the port of Montreal- no, not administered it, they have stripped it of a very substantial portion of revenue that should have come into the exchequer. By these men getting their position through appointment by this government, after the government had knowledge of their criminality and rascality, the revenues of the country have been filched. "Yes," they said to Mr. Clerk, 'we have found you unfaithful in little things, we will make you inspector over large things." That is the policy. This man's qualifications, Mr. Speaker, were simply a superb incompetence coupled with an elastic official conscience. He is a faithful political tool, nothing else. Why, they assigned one of the leading civil servants of Montreal to sit side by side with this man Clerk to do the routine work while Clerk was carrying on his criminal part in association with Bisaillon, covering up the tracks, keeping the officers here and there where they would be most useful to the smuggling ring. Thefts from the examining warehouse have been going on right along with his knowledge and with his participation. This man Clerk the acting minister appointed I believe-I was wrong a moment ago in saying the previous minister; I think it was the acting minister-this man he appointed to investigate the port of Montreal and make a report thereon to the government, a man associated intimately with those criminal smugglers in that district.
Now I take up the John W. Gaunt case by way of variation just to give an illustration of what was taking place. Here is a firm

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
that some, I suppose, will say was a responsible and respectable firm. I cannot agree with such a description because certain of their actions were reprehensible in the extreme. Mr. Gaunt, the head of the firm, received a thousand blank invoices from Holland, all properly certified. This country has certain laws respecting goods coming in from Germany and so forth. Goods were brought in from Germany. When the invoices arrived they would be transcribed on to these blank certified invoices at an under-valuation, passed through the customs, and only a remnant paid of the actual duty. The fraudulent practice was discovered. An expert accountant was appointed to check up, a man who knew thoroughly all about it-give us a chance and we will prove it-and he worked out these invoices and disclosed that the exchequer had been defrauded of $60,000 odd in duty. Gaunt left the country at a very opportune moment. The minister sitting now in his seat, the Acting Minister of Customs and Excise said "oh, do not be too hard on this man. Gaunt is a bad fellow, he is out of the country, but his partner is a gentleman." I believe he is, I have nothing to say against him at all. But why did not the government prosecute this case? Why was not fraud charged? Why were not the goods of the firm seized? Why *was not the exchequer recouped these frauds? No, Mr. Speaker, instead a legitimate claim of $60,000 odd was settled for $3,4001 I wonder if that was all it cost the Gaunt firm? I ask the government: Was that all it cost? That is all the records, I think, will disclose. But no prosecution for fraud, oh no. "Oh," the minister said, "if this man ever comes back-" No, it was the deputy minister The deputy pledged himself that if ever this man came back within the jurisdiction of the government he would be prosecuted for the fraud he had perpetrated. Has he been prosecuted? Has the government knowledge of this? Or do they pJead ignorance? Well, Sir, I say to the members of this House that if the government pleads ignorance of this also-of something that is known to all the officials of the department, of something that is known to scores of people in the country, of something that is open and clear to the world-if they plead ignorance, then it is abundant proof of their utter incapacity to hold office. Then they have no remnant of right to claim the confidence of this House, not a shred. No prosecution: nothing done in the case at all. Gaunt parades the streets.
Not only is that the case, Mr. Speaker, but I want to show that there are some officers in the department who are desirous of

doing their duty. But let me say this first. As soon as they knew they were discovered, the company got mighty busy a.nd shipped their goods out all over the country, anticipating the government would have the nerve and the sense of duty to prosecute them. But they were agreeably deceived. They emptied their warehouse of all but $20,000 worth of goods. Some officers of the department who were desirous of discharging their duty put a seal on that warehouse, and they said, "We will have this anyway for the exchequer." That was the action of honest officials of the department. Why did not the government keep those goods in their custody and so recoup the exchequer? They did not. The goods were released for a settlement of $3,400 -and the man who perpetrated the fraud comes back to Canada and presently walks the streets. Why do you not prosecute him now? Why have you not prosecuted him since you started this investigation. Oh, Mr. Speaker, this investigation is precisely what I said it was a moment ago, a mere farce. What for? I will tell the ministers what for. It is for this purpose, to gather all the evidence so they will know who the guilty people are, and then separate the sheep from the goats. But those on this list that I have in my hand will not be prosecuted. The arch conspirators, the chief smugglers, the men who deal in millions, will not be prosecuted-not if this government can get away with this adjournment. I will tell the House who will be prosecuted, perhaps-no, I doubt if even they will be prosecuted. There will be an odd official dismissed here, a fellow perhaps like Giroux who ought to be behind the bars, and Bisaillon who ought to have a life sentence. Bisaillon was fired; that was supposed to shut me up and end my investigation, but it is only started. These fellows will be fired and then the government will come before parliament-if we are foolish and simple enough to give them an adjournment-and say, "Oh, look what we have done; this man, that man, and the other man is gone." But that is not sufficient; the men who are defrauding this government of millions of dollars yearly and who have been doing so for years, will walk the streets as the chief henchmen, the political power behind the scenes of this government, and its supporters. That is where they will be.
Now I turn to another matter. I am not going into this question in detail, but I just wish to show that I am not dealing in ancient history. I hold in my hand freight bills for cars of liquor. I am not dealing with this question because of any views I may privately

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
hold as to the traffic in liquor, and I want this House to disabuse its mind of that;
I want the House to focus its attention on what I am saying. It is a question of whether the taxpayer of this country is having paid into the exchequer the revenues which ought to go there, in order that his taxes may be kept at the minimum, or whether by the connivance-or supine weakness of the government, to put it charitably-it has not been demonstrated that millions of dollars are being stolen from the exchequer and added to the burden of the taxpayer. That is the point. In this case, in the first three weeks of this year, half a dozen cars of liquor rolled out of the city of Montreal, with no evidence whatever that they paid the inland revenue tax. I say now, Mr. Speaker, that in one case I have under my hand-not in these few particular cases, but in these and others- literally hundreds of thousands of dollars have been taken yearly out of the exchequer of this country. I have the case which the minister is associated with, the sale of 16,000 gallons of alcohol which were seized. I know, Mr. Speaker, that the day after I put on the order paper a certain resolution calling for the papers, certain steps were taken to correct the documents in connection with this case. Instead of 16,000 gallons, there were something like 14,000; do not criticize me if I am out a few gallons. But after this alcohol was delivered to the Dominion Distillers; after my resolution appeared on the order paper; after it appeared that I knew something about the case, the Dominion Distillers asked that the count be corrected and that 400 gallons be added to the total. That may be an example of the exemplary honesty of these people. It may be that, but it looks to me, knowing a whole lot more about the incident, that it was simply a case of covering their tracks. But what was this alcohol sold for? This sixty-nine per cent over-proof alcohol was sold for thirty-six cents a gallon.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us the actual value?
I am just going to do that; I am going to let the Customs department tell me. A short time ago seventy drums of precisely the same stuff were sold by the Customs department for $14 a gallon.
That is with the excise added?

Exactly; I am going to
explain that. What is going to be the defence of the minister? First, that this was industrial alcohol. It was not. It was sixty-nine per
cent over-proof alcohol, precisely the same stuff as was previously sold by his own department for S14 a gallon-sold for thirty-six cents a gallon! The loss to the exchequer is over $260,000. There were no public tenders; there was no opportunity given the Quebec Liquor Commission; no chance given the Manitoba Liquor Board, nor the British Columbia Liquor Board; no chance given hospitals; no chance given the National Drug Company or the other big drug companies. It was sold to their friends for thirty-six cents a gallon. A previous seizure properly treated was sold for $14 a gallon. Do not say to me that the first included excise and the latter did not; I know it. I say, Mr. Speaker, that the 16,000 gallons-or what was left of it after some was stolen-ought to have been sold including excise; the excise is revenue to this government. But it will be said in defence, "Oh, but this was for export." They may bring documents showing some export of this stuff, but I say now that it was not exported and it was not bought for export. It was sold for thirty-six cents a gallon when it should have been sold for $14 a gallon. It was sold secretly and privately, when it should have been sold publicly. That is the statement. Not- only is that the case, Mr. Speaker, but these 16,000 gallons of spirit alcohol, worth over $200,000, were released from the king's warehouse by a telephone message. No warehouse receipt was surrendered; no order was given, simply a jingle of the phone, a familiar voice, and $200,000 worth of alcohol was turned loose. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the exchequer of Canada was defrauded in that deal alone of over $200,000, either by gross incompetence, or connivance.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few remarks on this amendment because I consider it is a very important one, and I am sure that when I return to my constituents the first thing they will ask me is how I conducted myself on this question of the adjournment that the government has tried to put through. Early in the afternoon and the evening I had what I considered very sufficient reasons for voting against this adjournment; but since the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. 'Stevens), those reasons are very much strengthened. This country owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre for bringing out the things that he did this evening. I was very much disappointed, as he proceeded with his remarks, to note the levity that was being exhibited by some hon. .members opposite. They did not seem to realize at all that this is a very serious charge that he is bringing against the administration, a charge that they will have to answer before the bar of public opinion. I am glad to see that a number of members of the Progressive party have realized their responsibility in this matter and have not shirked it. I can assure those hon. gentlemen who voted for the motion to adjourn the debate that they can go home to their constituents and present a much better report than had they voted the other way.
The Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) has made an excellent reply to those charges. He made it evidently on the spur of the moment and he dealt with some phases of them. But a number of things are still left to be dealt with, and this parliament and the country at large will insist upon their being dealt with right away. As a rule when the government bring in a motion .of this kind they take some steps to explain it to the satisfaction of members of parliament. But to-day we have seen a departure from that 'principle, and we have had no enlightenment whatever as to the reasons which have guided them in asking for this adjournment.

Adjournment-Customs Inquiry
Discrimination has been exhibited against the Conservative party in that regard, for evidently my hon. friends opposite passed out their information to gentlemen of the Independent group and gentlemen of the Progressive group. Is it fair or just that hon. gentlemen in this section of the House should be left in ignorance of reasons that have been given to other hon. gentlemen?
I have had a good deal of sympathy with the government during the time that this parliament has been sitting, because they have had to put up with so much from their allies, those who have been associated with them. Early in the war, when trenches were laid out rather indiscriminately, it was often the case that the line would go along in one direction and then back at an angle so that some of the men would be just behind their fellow soldiers and allies who occupied the line in front. Sometimes when those behind "got their wind up," as we used to say, and they saw any movement in our own trenches in front, they fired a volley, too. Now, that is what the allies of this government have been doing, the Labour group, the Independents, and the Progressives-practically every one of them has made some attack on the government that they are keeping going by their support, and it must be intensely humiliating for any administration with the slightest sdf-respect to continue in office under such circumstances.
I submit, Sir, that the country does not want an adjournment at the present time. The people expect parliament to function, to instil some stability into national affairs, and to my mind the very fact of asking for an adjournment to-day is an undoubted sign of weakness on the part of the government. I ask, why do they need time for reconstruction and for the preparation of legislation? What have they been doing in the interval that has elapsed since October 29 last-three solid months? They have had lots of time to prepare for the session, but they have done nothing in this direction because they have been too busy negotiating with the Progressives, otherwise they would have had something for us to consider now and it would not be necessary to ask for any adjournment.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is the ruler in this House, if he is not the leader.. That is recognized throughout the country, although it is also recognized that he has no qualifications for that position, nor any right to assume it. Every idea of the member for Brandon is parochial, I have never heard him express a national thought since I have been in this House, and I con-

sider that for the country to depend on him for leadership is entirely contrary to what should be the case. Liberalism used to be a strong force to be reckoned with; it is to-day outside the House, and in conversation with Liberals in my riding I have been impressed with the fact that they are humiliated and distressed by the conduct of their leaders in parliament. Let me give an example. The member for Hosetown (Mr. Evans) it was proved the other day made certain allegations during the recent campaign against the government, in the course of which he said that they were "wallowing in corruption," and he accused one minister of the crown of a vile untruth. In the old days the Liberal party would have resented that with all the power at their command. What do they do now? They meekly kiss his hand, and solicit his support. That is the attitude of the Liberal party to-day in parliament. In striking contrast we have the attitude of the Conservative party. It does not depend on any subterfuge, it does not ask for support from anyone unless he believes in its principles. The Conservative party stand for protection, it is the main article in its platform, and holding that policy it is opposed to any adjournment, as is also the country at large.

Mr. Speaker, while I am limited in parliamentary experience, yet I am one of the oldest members present, and I feel it is my duty to my constituents to express my strong opposition to the proposed adjournment. Although I have been in attendance since January' 7, I have not been able to do anything for my constituents or for my country, neither has any other member. To my mind it is regrettable that so much public time and public money should be wasted with so little result. Therefore I desire to express my strong disapproval of this motion, and I shall vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of grave concern to members of this House who have come here to transact public business to find that within less than a month a proposal is made by the government that parliament should adjourn for six weeks. I object to the motion, Sir, on the ground that it is a serious inconvenience to members that they ought not to be subjected to. There is no reason or justification given, in fact none can be given why such an adjournment should be taken. It has been pointed out in the strongest and most conclusive manner that there is plenty of material in the Speech from the
